nameStory: The "tridens" in this harvestman's scientific name means "three-toothed" in Latin, likely referring to three-pointed structures on the male's body. While it doesn't have a widely-used common name in North America, European naturalists sometimes call it the Three-toothed Harvestman. This species represents one of the less familiar harvestmen that have made their way from Europe to our New England forests.
description: The Three-toothed Harvestman is a small, delicate-looking arachnid with the characteristic long, thin legs that give harvestmen their "daddy longlegs" nickname. Unlike spiders, harvestmen have their body segments fused into what looks like a single oval pill with legs attached. This European native has established small populations in New England, where it quietly hunts tiny prey among leaf litter and low vegetation. Adults are typically small enough to sit comfortably on a dime.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, pill-shaped body that feels firm but not hard when gently touched, with no visible waist between body segments like you'd see on a spider

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small and delicate, with a body about the size of a peppercorn and legs that span roughly the width of a quarter

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Usually brownish or grayish coloration that blends with leaf litter, often with subtle darker patterns across the back

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves with a distinctive bouncing gait on its thread-like legs, often freezing motionless when disturbed rather than running away

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Two small, dark eyes positioned on a tiny bump or turret on top of the body, giving it an almost periscope-like appearance

habitat: Look for this harvestman in deciduous and mixed forests with rich, moist soil and plenty of decomposing leaf matter. They prefer areas with good ground cover like ferns, mosses, and low shrubs where they can hunt small insects and other tiny prey. In New England, they're most likely found in mature woodlands with diverse understory vegetation.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging as soil warms, often found under logs or in deep leaf litter where they've spent the winter months.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible and actively hunting. This is the best time to spot them moving through vegetation during cooler evening hours.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue to be active through early fall, preparing for winter by feeding heavily before cold weather arrives.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive, hiding deep in leaf litter, under bark, or in soil crevices to survive freezing temperatures.

funFact: These tiny harvestmen are incredibly effective pest controllers — they can reduce aphid populations by up to 97% in areas where they're active, making them gardeners' secret allies even though most people never notice them!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small harvestmen, but the Three-toothed Harvestman's compact size and subtle coloring help distinguish it. Remember: if it has a web, it's a spider; if it looks like a pill with legs and no web, it's a harvestman.
contextualKnowledge: Harvestmen are often called "daddy longlegs" but so are cellar spiders and crane flies, creating confusion. True harvestmen like this species are arachnids but cannot produce silk or venom, making them completely harmless to humans despite persistent myths about them being highly venomous.
compareHints: Since this is the only Oligolophus species documented in our region, compare it with other small harvestmen in the Phalangiidae family by looking for its particularly compact body size and subtle coloration. Most other New England harvestmen are either noticeably larger or have more distinctive markings and longer legs relative to their body size.
